Rehab In The Home enables eligible patients to receive rehabilitation care in their own homes, supporting recovery while reducing the need to travel for appointments. The expansion builds on the successful rollout of nurse practitioner-led wound care, continence and aged care outreach clinics in early 2025, which have experienced increasing demand. The expanded outreach and rehabilitation services will make it easier for older people, people living with disability or mobility challenges, and families to access the care they need closer to home. The community are now able to have their say on the proposed design and Review of Environmental Factors (REF) for the project, which is in response to longstanding calls from the local community for a direct connection between the Camden area and the Hume Motorway. This has meant motorists are forced to travel via Narellan Road, adding unnecessary time and distance to their journeys and putting additional pressure on this key road corridor as Camden continues to grow. records.substantive_excerpt: My Feed, My Way | Prime Minister of Australia Skip to main content My Feed, My Way Media release Tuesday 8 September 2026 The Hon Anthony Albanese MP Prime Minister of Australia The Hon Anika Wells MP Minister for Communications Minister for Sport Listen The Albanese Government is taking the next step following its world leading social media age ban to ensure Australians have more choice online, with draft legislation for the Digital Duty of Care released today for targeted consultation. These new laws will put the onus on digital service providers to provide a safe online environment, setting minimum standards for the features and tools they use. This will include an Australian first, “My Feed, My Way,” initiative which will give Australians control over their social media algorithms. Social media platforms will be required to send a notification to new and existing users offering them a choice over their default feed. Users can choose to opt in to having their default feed include personalised content recommended by the algorithm. Alternatively, users can opt out of personally recommended content in their default feed and see the friends and creators they choose to follow. This will give Australians greater choice over their platforms and what they see. Further, digital services like online games, apps and AI chatbots will be required to protect under 18s from design features that have negative behavioural impacts, like addictive features or those that can have an effect on a young person’s self-esteem. They will also be required to protect under 18s from harmful content like: content that promotes, encourages or accelerates eating disorders content that promotes hostile ideas about women and gender equality pornography content that glorifies crime or life endangering stunts content that causes serious mental health distress, including abuse and bullying. Australians will benefit from better protection from seriously harmful and illegal content across digital services, and social media users will be afforded more choice. The draft laws provide eSafety with the power to issue removal notices for nudify apps or websites, and streamline the child cyber-bulling and adult cyber abuse schemes to enable eSafety to deal more quickly with this harmful material. records.substantive_excerpt: Greens say Albanese must explain pork-barrelling claims at election inquiry | Australian Greens Skip to main content Search Search Greens say Albanese must explain pork-barrelling claims at election inquiry 2026-09-08 The Australian Greens are calling on the Prime Minister to urgently front up over reports that a $560 million Major and Local Community Infrastructure grants program was overwhelmingly directed to Labor-held and competitive electorates. Centre for Public Integrity analysis found no clear relationship between funding allocations and either community need or household income. One of the only golf clubs invited to apply was Marrickville Golf Club in the Prime Minister’s own electorate, which received $6 million. Greens spokesperson for Democracy, Senator Steph Hodgins-May, said the Prime Minister should front the Joint Standing Committee on Electoral Matters, which is currently conducting its inquiry into the 2025 federal election, and answer questions about the grant process himself. 'If you live or pay rates in Kinglake Ward, make sure you’re enrolled by 4 pm on Wednesday 23 September,' Mr Bluemmel said. 'Residents and ratepayers, as well as new citizens and people who have just turned 18, can check their enrolment or complete a new enrolment form online at vec.vic.gov.au .' New or updated enrolments must be received by 4 pm on Wednesday 23 September to count for the upcoming by-election. For more information on enrolment, voters can call 131 832 or visit vec.vic.gov.au , where they can also sign up to the free VoterAlert service to receive important election reminders by SMS and email. records.record_title: Key changes and improvements for the 2027 NSW State election released
records.substantive_excerpt: Key changes and improvements for the 2027 NSW State election released - NSW Electoral Commission Go to content language العربية Tiếng Việt 中文 Ελληνικά Italiano newspaper Media work Work with us contact_support Contact us search Search Menu Listen share Share Key changes and improvements for the 2027 NSW State election released On the International Day of Democracy, the NSW Electoral Commission published its 2027 NSW State Election Change Summary , highlighting key changes and improvements to how it will administer and regulate the upcoming State election. Shaped by legislative reform, stakeholder feedback, and the changing operating environment, the Change summary outlines how the Commission will deliver this major election event in line with its strategic goals of trusted delivery, strong regulation, and informed participation. Key changes and improvements for the 2027 State election include: Informed participation : expanding voting options for convenience and accessibility, enhanced education programs, attendance voting at correctional facilities, and a trial of low-sensory voting centres. Trusted delivery : prioritised ballot count efforts and increased transparency on count progress, improved staffing allocations and training, strengthened ballot paper security and tracking to protect election integrity. Strong regulation: new and changed rules for campaign finances and electoral materials, including regulation of digitally generated electoral material. NSW Electoral Commissioner Rachel McCallum said careful planning and preparation are always essential to delivering a major event of the scale and complexity of the NSW State election. “We are committed to ensuring election delivery considers the expectations of voters, candidates and the broader community as the electoral environment evolves” Commissioner McCallum said. "With the State election now only six months away, we aim to be transparent about our priorities, and how we preparing to deliver and regulate this major election event." “We continue to review and update our plans for the 2027 State election on 13 March. As we respond to any changes in the environment, we would encourage election participants, voters and anyone else with an interest in the administration of the 2027 NSW State election to engage with the Change summary.” The Electoral Commission has also released its Strategic Plan 2026/

records.substantive_excerpt: Defence Force Discipline Amendment (RCDVS Implementation and Related Measures No. 1) Bill 2026 – Parliament of Australia Skip to navigation Skip to content Defence Force Discipline Amendment (RCDVS Implementation and Related Measures No. 1) Bill 2026 Type Government Portfolio Defence Originating house House of Representatives Status Before Senate Parliament no 48 Track (What's this?) Permalink Summary Amends the: Defence Force Discipline Act 1982 to: implement certain recommendations of the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide in relation to suspension from duty while under investigation, sentencing procedures, disclosure of service offences, removing stigmatising language, and distinguishing between violent and non-violent commission of certain service offences; update superior tribunal procedures; establish the summary contravention scheme; and make a range of other amendments in relation to policing equipment, updates to prescribed quantities for drug offences, disclosure of investigative material, changes to service offences, changes to imprisonment terms for restricted courts martial and Defence Force magistrates, amendments to petition and for review processes, delegation of powers, functions of the Director of Military Prosecutions, harmonising termination grounds for judicial officers, application of territory rules of evidence, powers of investigating officers, and enabling removal orders for intimate images; Defence Force Discipline Act 1982 and Defence Force Discipline Appeals Act 1955 to: update powers for service tribunals when dealing with accused persons suffering from a mental impairment; and establish the Defence Mental Health Tribunal as a specialised decision-making body; Defence Act 1903 and Defence Force Discipline Act 1982 to update the title of ‘Director of Defence Counsel Services’ to ‘Director of Defence Legal Assistance’; and Administrative Decisions (Judicial Review) Act 1977 to extinguish convictions for historical homosexual service offences. The Contemporary Music Act 2026 is a landmark commitment under the NSW Government’s 10-year Contemporary Music Strategy and enshrines vital protections for music festivals, concerts and venues to uplift and promote the live music industry as a cornerstone of the state’s cultural identity and as a key employer and contributor to the economy: The legislation includes: Establishing a Music Venue Recognition Scheme: Will see a three-tier system set up to recognise ‘dedicated’, ‘significant’ and ‘live music’ venues. This will tailor the most effective government support – including extended trading hours and government grants. The scheme will also incentivise venues to host new, original live music regularly. The venue recognition scheme is expected to launch later this year. Updated definitions for concerts to support more local acts: Concert organisers will no longer be punished by being declared a ‘large scale music festival’ just because they hosted more than 4 acts at the same event. This supports local artists, local venues and local concert goers, and streamlines processes for organisers. New noise assessment methodology for outdoor events: Noise levels at music festivals and major events at Government sites including Centennial Park, the Domain and the Sydney Opera House will monitor sound using a standard average over time metric. This will cut the number of noise breaches for concerts and festivals due to a short burst of sound or even a gust of wind – which sees venues and organisers hit with extra costs. records.substantive_excerpt: Tough new powers to tackle organised crime pass NSW Parliament | NSW Government menu Open Menu MyServiceNSW Logged in MyServiceNSW Manage account Logout of MyServiceNSW Ministerial media release Tough new powers to tackle organised crime pass NSW Parliament Published: 25 September 2026 Released by: Attorney General, Minister for Police and Counter-terrorism Listen Legislation giving law enforcement stronger powers to investigate and disrupt organised crime and increasing penalties for those who facilitate serious offending have passed NSW Parliament. The Crimes and Other Legislation Amendment (Further Organised Crime Reforms) Bill 2026 passed Parliament last night. It included new powers for the NSW Crime Commission and NSW Police to combat organised crime. It also introduces tougher penalties for those who plan and facilitate organised crime murders and exposes children who carry out shootings or firebombings to adult maximum penalties. Strengthening the Crime Commission The package gives the Crime Commission the ability to compel suspects to hand over their digital devices immediately to prevent the destruction of crucial evidence. Previously, the Crime Commission could require someone to provide a device or document and bring it to a hearing. But it could not compel them to provide access at the point of being served a summons. The change means suspects will not be able to hide or destroy evidence in the lead up to a hearing. Those who refuse to comply face up to four years’ jail, a $4,400 fine or both and can be held in contempt of the Crime Commission. The legislation also doubles maximum penalties to 10 years for failing to comply with Crime Commission orders – including refusing to answer questions, obstructing investigations or giving false and misleading evidence. Previously, someone could only be ordered to unlock a device if it was seized as part of a search or crime warrant.
